power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Hand microvasculature is conventionally presented through diagrams, cadaveric atlases and specialized optical instruments, while conventional clinical radiography cannot resolve individual capillary loops (5-15 µm lumen) in vivo, which dominate cutaneous oxygen exchange.

We present Microcirculation Mirror, a zero-install browser workstation that registers layered hand anatomy to a live 21-landmark pose and couples it to a nailfold video capillaroscopy (NVC) simulator, a lumped microcirculatory model and an imaging-physics module.
The single-file application runs offline on a laptop or, over local HTTPS, on a phone as an installable app.
Results Its 3D atlas contains 136 named structures per hand in six systems from open Z-Anatomy/BodyParts3D meshes, plus a literature-parameterized capillary layer.
The NVC module renders a 200×, 1.2-mm field with six deterministic patterns and quantified density, giant capillaries, avascular width fraction, hemorrhages, tortuosity and ramification.

A lumped model reports nine estimates (SIM); a physics module shows that a 10-µm capillary occupies 0.07 of a 150-µm detector pixel; with iodinated contrast it retains ≈0.016% effective contrast, about 60× below a 1% detection threshold; unenhanced blood is ≈270× lower.
The 2D stage renders in 2.9 ms per frame; system merging reduces atlas draw calls from 136 to 6.
The camera-overlay layers are templates, the atlas macro-anatomy is open mesh data, and the capillary layer is sampled.
No patient data are used.
The instrument is a product prototype, not a medical device, and provides a reproducible framework for making multi-scale microvascular reasoning visible.
NOTE: This preprint reports new research that has not been certified by peer review and should not be used to guide clinical practice.
The microcirculation of the hand is studied across rheumatology, physiology and anatomy.
Rheumatologists examine nailfold capillary loops to identify the scleroderma pattern and distinguish its early, active and late stages [1] [2] [3].
text.formatted: Rheumatologists examine nailfold capillary loops to identify the scleroderma pattern and distinguish its early, active and late stages <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref> <ref type="bibr">[3]</ref>.

text.text: Physiologists investigate oxygen transport from capillaries measuring 5 to 15 µm in diameter to the surrounding tissue [4] [5] [6], while anatomists characterize the palmar arches and digital arteries supplying the skin [7, 8].
text.formatted: Physiologists investigate oxygen transport from capillaries measuring 5 to 15 µm in diameter to the surrounding tissue <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref>, while anatomists characterize the palmar arches and digital arteries supplying the skin <ref type="bibr">[7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">8]</ref>.

text.text: Despite these complementary perspectives, key microvascular structures and features, including capillary loops, the papillary plexus and the distinction between normal and abnormal nailfold architecture, remain difficult to visualize.

Individual capillaries cannot be resolved using conventional clinical radiography [9, 10], are generally inaccessible to surface microscopy outside the nailfold, and exhibit variability that cannot be adequately represented by a single static diagram.
text.formatted: Individual capillaries cannot be resolved using conventional clinical radiography <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">10]</ref>, are generally inaccessible to surface microscopy outside the nailfold, and exhibit variability that cannot be adequately represented by a single static diagram.

text.text: These limitations reflect a broader challenge in integrating anatomical information across spatial scales and imaging modalities.
Cadaveric dissection reveals macroscopic vascular anatomy but does not readily demonstrate individual capillary loops.
Two-dimensional atlases typically present the palmar arterial system and microvascular images separately, with limited spatial correspondence between them.

Clinical nailfold video capillaroscopy provides magnified views of the living nailfold, but its use depends on dedicated equipment, operator expertise and standardized acquisition procedures, including the fourfield protocol considered here.
Consequently, conventional anatomical resources and clinical capillaroscopy offer limited support for continuous exploration from a digital artery to the capillary bed it supplies.
Computational anatomy provides a potential framework for connecting these scales.
Open mesh collections, including BodyParts3D and Z-Anatomy, contain named three-dimensional models of the hand and forearm [11, 12].
text.formatted: Open mesh collections, including BodyParts3D and Z-Anatomy, contain named three-dimensional models of the hand and forearm <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[11,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">12]</ref>.

text.text: Browser-based hand tracking can estimate a pose comprising 21 landmarks from a single RGB frame [13], while Canvas2D and WebGL support the real-time rendering of layered anatomical annotations.
text.formatted: Browser-based hand tracking can estimate a pose comprising 21 landmarks from a single RGB frame <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[13]</ref>, while Canvas2D and WebGL support the real-time rendering of layered anatomical annotations.

text.text: Integrating these capabilities into a coherent interactive interface also requires clear differentiation among measured structures, anatomical templates, sampled features and simulated phenomena.
Recent preprints describing browser-based anatomy instruments provide related examples at comparable levels of evidence in anatomy and biomedical visualization [14, 15].
text.formatted: Recent preprints describing browser-based anatomy instruments provide related examples at comparable levels of evidence in anatomy and biomedical visualization <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[14,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">15]</ref>.

text.text: Microcirculation Mirror was developed to investigate whether a browser-based instrument could combine these capabilities within a single HTML file while preserving anatomical relationships and explicitly communicating the limitations of its visual representations.
The application registers skin, muscle, tendon, bone, nerve, artery, capillary and vein layers to a tracked hand and provides a separate three-dimensional hand atlas derived from open meshes.

It also renders a simulated nailfold video capillaroscopy field at 200-fold magnification with six selectable patterns, implements a lumped microcirculatory model, and uses attenuation and detector calculations to examine whether conventional clinical X-rays can resolve individual hand capillaries in vivo.
The application is designed to operate offline on a laptop or mobile phone without installation or reliance on a server-side database.
Our work presents the architecture and technical characterization of Microcirculation Mirror as a research and demonstration prototype.

Its contributions comprise a reproducible approach to poseregistered, multiscale microvascular anatomy in the browser, an open quantitative hand atlas that distinguishes mesh-derived anatomy from procedural microanatomy, and integrated simulation and imaging-physics modules that clarify both the basis and the limitations of the visualized information.
Evaluation is based on technical characterization and worked examples, consistent with the scope of a methods and instrument description.

The application is distributed as a single HTML file with embedded CSS and JavaScript and support for optional local assets, including a float16 hand-landmark model, six GLB layers per hand, and a compact Three.js build.
It requires no runtime build step, package manager, or server-side component.

The same file supports four operating modes, comprising a demonstration with an illustrative hand, camera-based tracking in which MediaPipe HandLandmarker estimates 21 landmarks [13], a full-screen three-dimensional atlas, and a microscopy and imaging-physics workspace (Fig. 1).
text.formatted: The same file supports four operating modes, comprising a demonstration with an illustrative hand, camera-based tracking in which MediaPipe HandLandmarker estimates 21 landmarks <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[13]</ref>, a full-screen three-dimensional atlas, and a microscopy and imaging-physics workspace (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1</ref>).

text.text: The interface maintains the hand as a shared spatial reference while allowing users to change anatomical layers and viewing scales.
The main stage presents the hand, while a panel on the right provides controls for anatomical layers, visualization settings, physiology, and numerical readouts.
Presets provide access to arterial, capillary, venous, musculoskeletal, and nailfold views.
Additional viewing controls allow users to alternate among a whole-field view, a split view, a lens centered on the index fingertip, a depth section, and a nailfold lens.

Selecting a visible vessel opens an inspector containing its anatomical name, vessel class, lumen diameter, depth, erythrocyte velocity, oxygen saturation (SO₂), wall shear stress, and segment length.
Rendering is organized into four coordinated canvases (Fig. 1c).
text.formatted: Rendering is organized into four coordinated canvases (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1c</ref>).

text.text: The shading canvas renders the skin envelope or camera veil, and the anatomy canvas renders bones, muscles, tendons, nerves, and lymphatics.
A WebGL or Canvas2D canvas renders arteries, capillaries, veins, and erythrocytes, while an annotation canvas presents labels, the viewing lens, scale bars, and the depth ruler.
All four canvases use the same landmark-derived pose, allowing the rendered layers to move together as hand position changes.
A lumped physiology model uses the shared application state to generate the nine numerical readouts presented in the control panel.
The tracker estimates 21 landmarks in screen coordinates, from which the application constructs orthogonal coordinate frames for the palm, four bone groups per digit, and the forearm.
The digital groups comprise 20 groups in total, with the thumb represented using its carpometacarpal-tometacarpophalangeal segment.
These frames are scaled according to tracked joint distances and smoothed using a frame-rate-aware exponential filter.
Temporary tracking losses are bridged for up to 18 frames before the overlay is cleared.
The resulting anatomical representation is pose-registered rather than segmented from the camera image.
Bones, muscles, tendons, and nerves are canonical templates whose geometry is derived from hand proportions (Fig. 2).
text.formatted: Bones, muscles, tendons, and nerves are canonical templates whose geometry is derived from hand proportions (Fig. <ref type="figure">2</ref>).

text.text: Anatomical layers can be viewed independently or in combination.
The arterial layer extends from the radial and ulnar arteries through the superficial and deep palmar arches to the common and proper palmar digital arteries, arterioles, and capillary loops.
The venous layer includes venules, dorsal digital veins, and the superficial and deep palmar venous networks.

The musculoskeletal layer represents the thenar and hypothenar eminences, interossei, lumbricals, and flexor tendons, while the neural layer depicts schematic median and ulnar nerve trunks and their digital branches.
An optional lymphatic layer provides a sparse, blind-ended network.
The skin envelope can be rendered as either a translucent veil or an opaque silhouette.
A depth-section view attenuates structures according to their modeled depth, while a circular lens centered on the index fingertip reveals the combined anatomical layers.
The vessel inspector provides quantitative information for individual vascular segments, including modeled lumen diameter, depth, erythrocyte velocity, oxygen saturation (SO₂), and wall shear stress.
Wall shear stress is calculated from the Poiseuille velocity profile as 𝜏 = 8𝜂𝑣/𝐷, with viscosity set to 𝜂 = 0.0035 Pa s.

All values are model estimates, and the inspector allows users to examine differences across vascular scales, including the nearly two-order-of-magnitude difference in diameter between a 0.9-mm proper palmar digital artery and a 10-µm capillary, together with their corresponding modeled velocities.
The true-scale view relates anatomical dimensions to the magnification required to make small structures visible.

In the default view, macrovascular diameters are shown at approximately 1-3 times their modeled size and capillary diameters at 30-60 times their modeled size, while the capillary bed is sampled well below its expected anatomical density.
At a scale of 1:1, a 10-µm capillary occupies approximately 0.02-0.05 pixels on a typical screen and therefore becomes a subpixel structure.

The resulting visualization illustrates a sampling limitation analogous to the detector-sampling constraints that, together with limited attenuation contrast, prevent conventional clinical radiography from resolving individual capillary loops in vivo.
The 3D atlas is a separate full-screen viewer built from the Z-Anatomy collection, with geometry derived from BodyParts3D [16].
text.formatted: The 3D atlas is a separate full-screen viewer built from the Z-Anatomy collection, with geometry derived from BodyParts3D <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[16]</ref>.

text.text: The hand subset comprises 136 named structures per hand across six anatomical systems, including 29 bones, 14 joint capsules and ligaments, 47 muscles, fasciae, and tendon sheaths, 13 arterial segments, 10 venous segments, and 23 nerve segments (Fig. 3).

text.text: The skeletal structures include the radius, ulna, eight carpals, five metacarpals, and fourteen phalanges.

Each structure is annotated with English and Chinese names and mesh statistics (Supplementary Fig. 6); 36 structures also have a Foundational Model of Anatomy (FMA) identifier, and 26 include a brief description.

text.text: The left and right hands are extracted independently.
The atlas contains seven independently controlled layers representing the skeleton, ligaments and joints, muscles and sheaths, arteries, veins, nerves, and procedural microvasculature.
Visibility and opacity can be adjusted for each layer.
A two-stage exploded-view control first separates anatomical systems and then individual structures, while a cutaway plane clips the model along the X, Y, or Z axis.
Search supports English names, Chinese names, and FMA identifiers.
Selecting a structure opens an inspector showing its name, anatomical system, FMA identifier, bounding-box dimensions, and mesh counts.
Seven viewing presets, palmar, dorsal, radial, ulnar, proximal, distal, and oblique, and a 26second guided tour provide reproducible viewpoints.
Switching between hands loads the corresponding set of six GLB files.
Neither source dataset includes capillary, arteriole, or venule meshes.
The microvascular layer is therefore generated at runtime on the volar surfaces of the five distal phalanges, with approximately 12 loops per fingertip and 60 loops per hand.

Loop geometry is informed by published morphometry, including a loop height of 278.5 ± 53.3 𝜇m and limb diameters of 5.6-13.4 µm from volar-digit measurements [17], together with an outer loop width of approximately 39 µm [18].

text.text: The layer supports magnifications of 1, 10, and 20 times and is labeled "sampled for legibility".

At unit magnification, loop height and width follow the published dimensions and become subpixel at the viewing scale used, whereas tube diameter remains exaggerated at all magnifications to preserve visibility.
The resulting geometry is an illustrative model.
Provenance is documented throughout the atlas.
Macro-anatomical structures use reference mesh data, whereas microvascular structures are procedurally generated.

text.text: The physics module evaluates whether conventional clinical X-ray imaging can resolve individual capillaries in the living hand.
Under the imaging conditions considered, capillary visibility is limited by insufficient attenuation contrast and inadequate spatial sampling (Fig. 7).
text.formatted: Under the imaging conditions considered, capillary visibility is limited by insufficient attenuation contrast and inadequate spatial sampling (Fig. <ref type="figure">7</ref>).

text.text: For unenhanced blood, the primary limitation is the small attenuation difference between blood and surrounding soft tissue.
At 60 keV, their mass attenuation coefficients are approximately 0.2053 and 0.2025 cm 2 /g , respectively, corresponding to a difference of approximately 1.4% [9].
text.formatted: At 60 keV, their mass attenuation coefficients are approximately 0.2053 and 0.2025 cm 2 /g , respectively, corresponding to a difference of approximately 1.4% <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[9]</ref>.

text.text: With respective densities of 1.06 and 1.03 g/ cm 3 , the linear attenuation coefficients differ by approximately 0.009 cm -1 , or 4.4%.
A 1-mm column of unenhanced blood therefore produces approximately 0.09% transmission contrast, whereas a 10-µm capillary produces approximately 9 × 10 -4 % before pixel averaging.
Averaging within a 150-µm pixel reduces the estimated contrast to approximately 6 × 10 -5 %.
Iodinated contrast material at 350 mg I/mL increases the linear attenuation difference to approximately 2.44 cm -1 , more than two orders of magnitude above that of unenhanced blood.
The corresponding transmission contrasts are approximately 21.7% for a 1-mm vessel, 4.8% for a 200-µm vessel, and 0.24% for a 10-µm vessel.

After averaging within a 150-µm pixel, the estimated contrast of the 10-µm vessel falls to approximately 0.016%, about 60 times below the representative 1% DSA detection threshold used in the analysis.
Contrast enhancement therefore does not overcome the combined effects of small vessel diameter and pixel averaging under these conditions.
Spatial sampling imposes an additional constraint.
Clinical digital radiography and computed radiography detectors typically have pixel pitches of 100-200 µm, corresponding to Nyquist frequencies of 2.5-5 line pairs/mm.

Sampling a 10-µm vessel across two pixels would require a pixel pitch of no more than 5 µm, corresponding to approximately 100 line pairs/mm and a sampling frequency 20-40 times higher than that of these clinical detectors.
DSA can demonstrate arteries approximately 200 µm in diameter [26], but does not resolve individual capillary loops measuring 5-15 µm.
text.formatted: DSA can demonstrate arteries approximately 200 µm in diameter <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[26]</ref>, but does not resolve individual capillary loops measuring 5-15 µm.

text.text: Clinical CT generally provides coarser spatial resolution of approximately 0.5-0.7 mm, although ultra-high-resolution photoncounting CT can approach 150 µm.
In the modeled CT scenario, partial-volume dilution reduces the signal from a 39-µm loop to well below 1 HU, beneath typical CT noise levels.
Even the less stringent criterion of separating adjacent loops remains unmet under the assumed clinical sampling conditions.

An inter-capillary spacing of approximately 143 µm requires sampling at intervals of no more than 72 µm, corresponding to approximately 7 line pairs/mm and exceeding the sampling capabilities considered for clinical DR/CR, DSA, and CT.

text.text: Microcirculation Mirror integrates multiscale anatomical exploration, representation of evidence provenance, and imaging-physics calculations within a browser-based instrument.

These capabilities address a challenge in microvascular visualization, namely the difficulty of relating macroscopic vascular anatomy to microscopic structures while preserving spatial context and communicating the evidential basis of each representation.

The principal contribution is therefore not any individual visualization, but an integrated environment in which users can examine anatomical relationships, explore simulated mechanisms, and inspect the limitations of the displayed information.
The instrument supports continuous exploration across anatomical scales.
Users can begin with the palmar arches on a tracked hand, follow the digital arteries, visualize the capillary bed, and open a simulated nailfold field.
Enabling the true-scale view illustrates how individual capillaries become smaller than a single pixel.
A shared hand reference, coordinate framework, and interaction model connect structures spanning nearly three orders of magnitude in vessel diameter.
Unlike static illustrations or conventional atlases, the integrated environment maintains spatial and interactive continuity as users move between scales.
Pose registration therefore offers a means of linking anatomical levels that are typically presented separately, although its educational value remains to be established empirically.
An equally important feature is the clear identification of information sources and their evidential status.

The interface differentiates tracked hand pose from template anatomy, mesh-derived structures from procedural capillaries, published reference values from model estimates, and simulated patterns from patient images.
Information about provenance is integral to interpreting the visualizations, not merely supplementary annotation.

Labeling bones as templates, the capillary bed as a sampled representation, and the Krogh field as a normalized visual approximation helps prevent visual realism from being mistaken for subject-specific accuracy.
Simulation makes selected mechanisms and assumptions available for examination, while source labels clarify that the visualizations do not represent clinical measurements.
The integration of imaging physics extends the instrument beyond anatomical visualization.
The limitations of conventional clinical radiography are examined through attenuation coefficients, detector sampling, and true-scale visualization.

Under the assumptions used in the module, a 10-µm capillary occupies approximately 0.02-0.05 pixels at true scale, while its effective contrast after pixel averaging is approximately 0.016% when filled with iodinated contrast material; the corresponding contrast for unenhanced blood is approximately 270 times lower.
These estimates illustrate how vessel dimensions, attenuation differences, and spatial sampling jointly constrain visibility.

They also contextualize the use of nailfold video capillaroscopy, optical coherence tomography, and side stream dark-field imaging for microvascular observation, alongside emerging applications of photoacoustic imaging and ultrasound localization microscopy.
The calculations apply to the specified conventional clinical imaging conditions and do not establish a universal limit on X-ray visualization of capillary-scale vessels.
These contributions must be interpreted within the scope of a prototype that has neither incorporated patient data nor undergone clinical validation.
The anatomical layers are pose-registered templates, the vascular network is schematic, and the capillary bed is sampled at a density substantially below that of the represented tissue.
The nailfold visualization is limited to a single illustrative 1.2-mm field and does . not constitute a complete four-field clinical acquisition.
The six simulated patterns are generated from literature-informed parameters, with no patient measurements used in their construction.
Physiological outputs are derived from a lumped model without individual calibration, and the microvascular flow index and heterogeneity index are empirical approximations.
The application is not a medical device and must not be used for diagnosis, screening, risk stratification, or treatment decisions.
These limitations informed the interface design, particularly the separation of tracked, template-based, and simulated content.
The present evaluation is restricted to technical characterization, including structural coverage, frame time, draw calls, file size, imaging-physics calculations, and simulator determinism.
It does not establish usability, educational benefit, or agreement with a clinical reference standard.
Further evaluation could compare learning outcomes or task performance between users of the instrument and users of a conventional atlas.
Think-aloud studies could examine how users interpret true-scale views and whether provenance labels support accurate understanding of reference anatomy and simulated content.

Expert review of the simulated nailfold patterns could assess their morphological plausibility and consistency with the intended categories, but would not constitute clinical validation of the classification system.
Landmark registration should also be evaluated against an independent marker-based reference.
Deterministic pattern generation, structured JSON export, and single-file deployment provide a basis for reproducible testing, although these studies have not yet been conducted.
Greater anatomical fidelity represents another direction for development.
The current instrument combines open reference meshes for macro-anatomy with procedural representations of microanatomy.

Incorporating subject-specific optical coherence tomography or nailfold video capillaroscopy data, or replacing the procedural capillary bed with a micro-CT-derived scaffold, would move the corresponding layer toward an image-derived anatomical model.
These extensions would require revised provenance labels and validation procedures appropriate to the acquisition and reconstruction methods.

The modular capillary layer and system-level provenance metadata provide an architectural basis for incorporating acquired nailfold fields, segmented optical coherence tomography volumes, and patient-specific meshes while preserving information about the origin and processing of acquired and simulated content.
The deployment approach may also broaden access to computational anatomy.

A single HTML file designed to run offline on a laptop or phone, without installation or a patient-data workflow, reduces some of the infrastructural requirements associated with conventional visualization platforms.
The documented deployment pathway using a local network, HTTPS, token-based access, and progressive web application functionality is intended to support reproducible demonstrations.
It allows the same instrument to be shared with research or clinical teams without requiring a vendor platform, license server, or cloud account.
The MIT-licensed code and CC BY-SA atlas further support reuse within their respective licensing conditions.

Taken together, these features position Microcirculation Mirror as a research and demonstration instrument and as an architectural reference for computational anatomy projects that seek to combine interactive visualization with communication of evidential limits.
Microcirculation Mirror remains a research and demonstration prototype with limitations in anatomical sampling, model formulation, and technical implementation.
The macroscopic view includes . approximately 12 capillary loops per fingertip and 60 per hand, a sparse representation that does not reproduce tissue-level capillary density or network topology.
The rule-based categorization of the six simulated nailfold patterns is not a validated implementation of Fast Track or CAPI-score and is intended only for illustration.

The visualized Krogh field is normalized and radially exaggerated, with the analytical solution provided separately for comparison; its spatial extent and gradients therefore do not constitute quantitative predictions of tissue oxygenation.
The empirical microvascular flow and heterogeneity indices have likewise not been validated against measurement-based indices.
Atlas rendering remains constrained by CPU rasterization, and the optimized rendering path does not eliminate the need for GPU acceleration for efficient performance.
The application supports tracking of only one hand at a time, while camera-based operation on mobile phones requires WebGL and HTTPS.
Single-file deployment simplifies distribution but does not guarantee equivalent functionality or performance across devices and browsers.

MediaPipe returns 21 landmarks per hand in normalized image coordinates.

The application mirrors the x coordinate for the front camera, converts to display coordinates, applies an object-fit: cover mapping when the video aspect differs from the stage, and smooths the landmarks with an exponential filter whose time constant is frame-rate aware.
From the smoothed landmarks it builds a palm frame (wrist, index MCP, little MCP), sixteen bone frames (four per finger) and a forearm frame.
Each frame is an orthonormal basis scaled by the distance between its defining joints.
Detections are considered lost after 18 consecutive frames without a hand; the overlay is then cleared.
The camera overlay's anatomy is generated procedurally from canonical hand proportions and the tracked frames.
The 3D atlas is extracted from the Z-Anatomy Startup.blend (Blender 3.6.5) with a righthand region 𝑥 ∈ [-0.38, -0.15], 𝑦 ∈ [-0.12,0.10], 𝑧 ∈ [0.69,1.00] m and a left-hand region mirrored in x.

Mesh and curve objects in the Skeletal, Joints, Muscular, Cardiovascular and Nervous collections are evaluated, world transforms are baked, the proximal end is clipped at 𝑧 = 1.00 m, and one GLB is exported per system with one node per structure.
Metadata are written to atlas-meta.json; the left-hand set is a separate extraction.
The capillary layer is generated at run time from the literature parameters in Supplementary Fig. 2b.
text.formatted: The capillary layer is generated at run time from the literature parameters in Supplementary Fig. <ref type="figure">2b</ref>.

text.text: The NVC field is 1.2 mm wide with 1 mm = 500 px.

Loop spacing is 1/𝜌, where 𝜌 is the pattern density in loops/mm; avascular gaps are one to four contiguous intervals whose total width is proportional to the avascular fraction; each loop receives a seeded morphology (hairpin, tortuous, bushy, ramified or giant); giant loops are forced for SSc patterns; haemorrhages are drawn as sub-papillary deposits; and loop width, height and perfusion are modulated by the physiological state.
The random seed is deterministic per pattern and index.
Metrics are computed from the generated field and reported with the pattern profile, reference ranges and a non-diagnostic disclaimer.
The model is defined by the equations in the Results and in Supplementary Fig. 2.
text.formatted: The model is defined by the equations in the Results and in Supplementary Fig. <ref type="figure">2</ref>.

text.text: The Hill parameters are 𝑃50 = 26.6 mmHg and 𝑛 = 2.7 .
The Krogh display uses a normalised radial approximation,.
Capillary recruitment adjusts the number of loops represented as perfused in the visualization and does not imply a change in anatomical capillary density.
The flow index is 0.05(𝑇 -33))(1 -0.30𝑆 sym )(0.55 + 0.45𝑅), and blood flow is 𝑄 = clamp(6.4𝐼, 0.8,12) mL/100 g/min.
Erythrocyte velocity follows a Poiseuille-like scaling, 𝑣 = clamp(0.85(𝑄/4.5) 0.60 (0.65 + 0.35𝑅), 0.08, 1.8) mm/s.
Fig 1 A zero-install instrument for multi-scale hand microvascular anatomy. a, Spatial resolution of imaging modalities on a logarithmic scale.

The shaded band marks the 5-15-µm capillary lumen; optical modalities (SDF/IDF, NVC, OCT, photoacoustic) reach it, while conventional radiography, DSA and laboratory micro-CT do not in routine clinical use. b, The application running on an illustrative palm: a 21-landmark pose registers skin, bone, muscle, tendon, nerve, artery, capillary and vein layers in real time. c, System architecture.
Camera input or an illustrative palm provides the basis for a 21-landmark pose represented in the Media Pipe format.
A pose rig comprising the palm, four bone groups per digit, and the forearm supports rendering across four canvases for shading, anatomy, vessels, and the heads-up display (HUD).
A physiology model incorporating flow, Hill, and Krogh formulations supplies modelderived readouts alongside the nailfold video capillaroscopy (NVC) and cross-sectional views. d, Frame budget.

The 2D stage renders in 2.9 ms and the nailfold field in 1.0 ms against the 16.7-ms budget for 60 fps. e, Module coverage matrix. f, Thumbnails of the lens reveal, nailfold field, 3D atlas and phone layout.
All screenshots are from the application.
SIM indicates model estimates.
